source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Exp 1: people rate a matching fact that sits inside a shared causal system as better support for an analogy than an equally good isolated match.
numbers: Exp 1, 48 subjects. Ratings of shared-system vs different-system key facts: analogy group 6.28 vs 4.89; target-only control 5.22 vs 5.31. Condition x fact-type F'(1,44)=13.99, p<.001. Choice task: analogy group chose the shared-system fact 3.17 of 4 times vs control 2.0, F(1,44)=18.43. Per passage 67-92% vs 42-54% for control.
limits: Short written passages. The target-only control rules out that the shared-system fact was simply more salient.
agent_relevance: Rank candidate inferences by whether they hang off a causal chain the source and target share (O7 check).

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Exp 2: asked to predict a new fact about the target, people predict the one tied to the shared causal system, not an equally plausible isolated one.
numbers: Exp 2, 32 subjects, 4 passages. Shared-minus-different-system predictions per subject: analogy group 1.63, target-only 0, F(1,28)=20.05, p<.001. Choice task: 2.9 vs 1.8 of 4, F(1,28)=16.43. Rating interaction F'(1,9)=10.99, p<.01. Still significant with one possibly biased passage removed, F(1,28)=13.03.
limits: Both candidate facts were in the base, plausible in the target and had antecedents there. Other answers were common (shared and different system do not exhaust responses).
agent_relevance: Candidate inferences are selected by structural support, not plausibility alone. Our agent should test for it.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Exp 3 repeated Exp 2 with the base passage out of view (memory only). Effect held but was weaker.
numbers: Exp 3, 48 subjects, 3 passages. Shared-minus-different predictions: analogy 0.92 vs target-only 0.13, F(1,44)=5.15, p<.05. Choice: 1.875 vs 1.0 of 3, F(1,44)=13.15. Rating interaction F(1,44)=10.82, p<.01. Passage 2 did not follow the pattern because memory of that base passage was poor on its comprehension test.
limits: Same-lab replication, not independent. Weaker because subjects did not always hold an accurate record of the base.
agent_relevance: If the source is paraphrased or dropped from context, structure-guided inference weakens. Keep the source text in view when inferring.

source: Clement & Gentner (1991) Systematicity as a selection constraint in analogical mapping
finding: Subjects who chose shared-system predictions justified them by the matching causal structure, not by the single fact matching.
numbers: Coded free-text justifications in Exp 1-3 (Tables 7 and 10): few were about the fact-to-fact match alone.
limits: Self-report; authors treat as supporting, not proof.
agent_relevance: Ask the model to name the shared causal chain that licenses each transferred conjecture.

source: Markman (1997) Constraints on analogical inference
finding: Exp 1 (school departments): subjects inferring from a base school to a target school listed more shared-system causal facts than nonshared ones.
numbers: Exp 1, 32 subjects. Mean inferences per item: shared-system 0.52, nonshared 0.22 (t(31)=3.97, p<.01), other (not in base) 0.56. Inference type F(2,60)=6.28, p<.01. Shared vs other not reliable.
limits: Small mean counts. Unexpectedly many 'other' inferences. Blind rater coded.
agent_relevance: People also invent facts beyond the source; code should tag candidates as copied vs invented.

source: Markman (1997) Constraints on analogical inference
finding: Exp 2: clearer shared-system bias in a redesigned study with 60 subjects.
numbers: Exp 2, 60 subjects. Per trial: shared-system 1.26 vs nonshared 0.30 (t(59)=7.32, p<.001) vs other 0.58 (t(59)=4.35). Type F(2,116)=30.49. More shared-system inferences came from departments the subject had mapped (0.77 vs 0.50, t(59)=2.87); interaction F(1,58)=16.01.
limits: Nonshared facts always outnumbered shared-system facts, so the bias is not due to availability.
agent_relevance: Strong support that systematicity filters candidate inferences.

source: Markman (1997) Constraints on analogical inference
finding: Exp 3 and 3a: shared-system inference bias held with the base in memory.
numbers: Exp 3, 48 subjects: shared 1.45 vs nonshared 0.39 (t(46)=6.23, p<.001), F(2,86)=30.87. Exp 3a, 78 subjects: shared 1.41 vs nonshared 0.36 (t(77)=7.20); correct department pair mapped by 85% (66/78); two departments with no shared facts mapped by 12% (9/78).
limits: Chain valence changed counts in Exp 3 (F(1,43)=5.87) but the direction flipped in 3a; authors could not explain it. Within-paper replication only.
agent_relevance: Consistent across four experiments, but same author and design family.

source: Markman (1997) Constraints on analogical inference
finding: People kept one-to-one mapping in inference: no inconsistent object substitutions in any of four studies, and causal chains stayed separate.
numbers: Zero inconsistent substitutions across Exp 1-3a. Exp 2: chains kept distinct in 46 of 50 (92%) cases, mixed 3 times (6%). Exp 3: 5 of 24 (21%) mixed. Exp 3a: 5 of 44 (11%).
limits: Few conflict opportunities; small counts.
agent_relevance: Supports a code check that no source element maps to two target elements. Cheap to implement.

source: Markman (1997) Constraints on analogical inference
finding: Systematicity is one constraint, not the only one. Salience (causal beats temporal relations, Lassaline 1996) and pragmatic goals also steer which facts are carried over.
numbers: Cited in Markman: with free prediction 53% of predictions were the shared-system fact, 22% unshared base facts, 18% other; controls named a key fact only 18% of the time. Spellman & Holyoak (1996) soap-opera plot extensions nearly always kept character correspondences.
limits: Second-hand summary of other studies; I opened Markman, not the originals.
agent_relevance: A stated goal should narrow candidate inferences; do not rely on structure alone.

source: Markman (1997) Constraints on analogical inference
finding: Compares SME, ACME, LISA and other models on inference. Pure copy-with-substitution is too profligate; SME needed a pragmatic marking step to restrict inferences.
numbers: No numbers. Argues the analogical inference process is conservative and its outputs must be checked by a separate process for factual truth.
limits: Qualitative model discussion.
agent_relevance: Matches our O7 design: generate candidates, filter by structure, then verify with a separate check.

source: Colhoun & Gentner (2009) Inference processes in causal analogies
finding: Replicated Lee & Holyoak (2008) Exp 1: a shared preventer lowers the effect inference while it raises similarity.
numbers: Study 1A, 70 undergraduates. Similarity: GGP 7.53, GG 6.35, GP 5.01 (F(2,286)=44.4). Effect-inference rating: GG 89.4, GGP 74.4, GP 46.1 (F(2,270)=164.6, p<.0001).
limits: Only one effect inference tested; sparse animal descriptions.
agent_relevance: Overall similarity is a poor stand-in for trust in one specific inference.

source: Colhoun & Gentner (2009) Inference processes in causal analogies
finding: A rival lab's reading: counting ALL candidate inferences, inductive strength follows similarity, so no dissociation from structure mapping.
numbers: Study 1B, 22 undergraduates. Mean proportion of inferences endorsed: GGP .81, GG .54, GP .41 (F(2,174)=142.3, p<.0001). Effect inference alone: GGP .65, GG .86, GP .18.
limits: Small N. Categorical endorsement differs from the rating format. This is an argument in an ongoing dispute with Lee & Holyoak.
agent_relevance: Track both single-inference confidence and whole-mapping strength; they can diverge.

source: Colhoun & Gentner (2009) Inference processes in causal analogies
finding: Study 2: effect ratings did not depend on whether the causal relations were stated in the base or in the target, so the base supplies the causal model.
numbers: Study 2, 32 undergraduates in 4 groups (n=9-11). No-analogy vs target-relations vs base-relations: group F(2,56)=.55 n.s.; interaction F(4,56)=.77 n.s.; target type F(2,56)=56.1. Stating the effect in the base raised ratings for GP and GPP targets.
limits: Tiny groups; null results; authors note a possible trend for the GP target in the base-relations group.
agent_relevance: Supports separating transfer of the causal model from a later ordinary causal check on it.

source: Colhoun & Gentner (2009) Inference processes in causal analogies
finding: Study 3: SME plus a simple post-analogical causal calculation matched Lee & Holyoak's human data closely.
numbers: Close fit reported by authors; no single fit statistic quoted in the text I read.
limits: Authors' own model, fit to published data, not blind.
agent_relevance: Keep transfer and truth evaluation as two separate steps in code.

source: Lee & Holyoak (2008) The role of causal models in analogical inference (as described by Colhoun & Gentner)
finding: Claim: causal models guide analogical inference; preventers change the effect inference without changing similarity.
numbers: Not read first hand. Described by Colhoun & Gentner as animal pairs with generative and preventative causes.
limits: Contested by Colhoun & Gentner (2009). Not opened.
agent_relevance: A rival account to keep in view: unified causal-model theory vs structure mapping plus causal reasoning.

source: Lassaline (1996) Structural alignment in induction and similarity (as described by Colhoun & Gentner and Markman)
finding: Inductive strength rises with more shared structure; binding causal relations add strength; causal relations are more salient than temporal ones.
numbers: Not opened. Described in two opened papers only.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Score candidate inferences by how many shared antecedents they attach to.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat college students on text matrices, letter strings and verbal analogies, but was worse on story analogies.
numbers: Story analogies: students clearly better, OR=0.37, p=0.0003, CI 0.21-0.63; 15 of 54 students picked the analogous story on every trial. 57 UCLA undergraduates on letter strings. GPT-4 in an initial test was much stronger on stories.
limits: Contamination of benchmarks possible; authors say GPT-3 did not learn analogy in a human way.
agent_relevance: Recognising an analogy is easy for strong LLMs when relations are simple; story-level relations are harder.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Gick-Holyoak radiation problem: GPT-3 alone gave a wrong fix; given the general story it found convergence and explained the correspondences; with distractor stories it failed until told to consider earlier stories.
numbers: Qualitative; one clinical problem plus a child gumball task where GPT-3 gave mechanically nonsensical solutions.
limits: Handpicked cases, no rates.
agent_relevance: Solution transfer works when the source is in context but needs a prompt to retrieve among distractors. Supply the source explicitly.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Letter-string analogies with permuted alphabets: humans stay high, GPT models fall sharply, so Webb et al.'s success partly reflects training overlap.
numbers: 136 human participants (Prolific); GPT-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. Error types (percent of errors, GPT-3 / GPT-4 / human): incorrect rule 30.97 / 32.67 / 14.67; completely wrong 7.74 / 2.67 / 12.50.
limits: Per-condition accuracy table columns could not be matched from the text extraction; see paper figures.
agent_relevance: Analogy and rule transfer by LLMs is brittle when surface form is unfamiliar.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Robustness tests: GPT models drop on variants of letter-string and (one type of) digit-matrix tasks; on story analogies GPT-4 shows answer-order bias and paraphrase sensitivity.
numbers: Stories: GPT-4 0.75 (27/36, Webb et al.) and 0.86 (31/36, theirs). Answer first 1.0 (18/18) vs second 0.72 (13/18). Humans 0.78 first, 0.78 second (564/720 overall). Paraphrased correct story: GPT-4 0.86 to 0.72 (26/36). Human trials: 1,876 letter-string; 1,550 digit-matrix original.
limits: Their GPT-4 results on digit matrices replicated WHL closely; only one of two variants hurt LLMs.
agent_relevance: Randomise answer order and paraphrase whenever an LLM judges how a source maps to a target.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere & Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: Mapping a semantic source to symbol patterns and inferring the missing target element: LLMs were order-sensitive and distractor-sensitive in Study 1, and the best LLM matched humans in Study 2.
numbers: Permuted Pairs drops LLM performance: Claude 3 coef -1.78 (z=-4.22), GPT-4 -1.68 (z=-3.98), Llama-405B -2.34 (z=-5.50), all p<.001; humans unaffected. Study 2: best LLM equals humans in all conditions and exceeds them on compositional variants.
limits: Authors conclude LLMs likely use different mechanisms. Performance rises with MMLU score.
agent_relevance: Inferring a target element from a source mapping is feasible but order-fragile; randomise pair order.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer & Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: LLMs spot near analogies but fail far system analogies, especially next to surface-similar distractors.
numbers: Humans 96% overall vs models 57%. Near analogies: humans 97.9%, models 75.0%. Far analogies: humans 94.1%, models 39.6% (below the 50% chance). Best GPT-4 mean 68.1%; SBERT 42.3%. Far analogy against near distractor: models 33.9%.
limits: Telling models to attend to system mappings did not fix the near-distractor case. Narrative classification, not inference generation.
agent_relevance: A surface-similar but structurally wrong source gives wrong transferred conjectures. Add structure checks and decoy tests.

source: Sourati, Ilievski, Sommerauer & Jiang (2024) ARN: Analogical Reasoning on Narratives
finding: What helped: few-shot far-analogy demonstrations and step-by-step reasoning gave modest gains; near-analogy demos were harmful in places.
numbers: Tested 0, 2, 4, 6 solved demonstrations on Llama-2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4; increasing far-analogy demos gradually improved detection of near analogies; best model still only halfway between chance and humans even with few-shot.
limits: Exact per-condition percentages not extracted. Expense limited GPT-4 tests.
agent_relevance: Prompt examples of far analogies may help a little; do not expect they close the gap.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Prompting the model to recall its own related problems before solving (analogical prompting) beat 0-shot and few-shot CoT on code generation, with modest gains.
numbers: Codeforces (Acc@1 / Acc@10), GPT-3.5-turbo-16k: 0-shot 8/24, 0-shot CoT 9/27, 3-shot CoT 11/27, self-generated exemplars 13/25, exemplars plus knowledge 15/29. GPT-4: 16/30, 16/29, 17/31, 17/32, 19/37. GPT-3.5 with the method 15% vs GPT-4 baseline 16% Acc@1.
limits: Authors state it fails if the model lacks relevant knowledge, suits stronger models, uses more output tokens and is prompt-sensitive.
agent_relevance: Self-made analogies help a little; test as an optional operator, not a core step.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Retrieved real exemplars beat self-generated ones for small models, self-generated won for large models (GSM8K).
numbers: Table 4 compares 0-shot CoT, 5-shot retrieved CoT and self-generated exemplars across model scales; per-cell values not extracted.
limits: Authors state the effect depends on model strength.
agent_relevance: For a weak model, ground analogies in an external verified source instead of self-made ones.

source: Wijesiriwardene et al. (2023) ANALOGICAL: a benchmark for long text analogy evaluation in LLMs
finding: Benchmark of six levels of long-text analogy (word, word vs sentence, syntactic, negation, entailment, metaphor); identifying analogies gets harder up the taxonomy.
numbers: Thirteen datasets, three distance measures, eight LLMs; per-level numbers not extracted.
limits: Measures embedding-space similarity, not candidate-inference generation. Abstract and skim only.
agent_relevance: Weak direct relevance to O7; shows deeper relations are harder to align.

source: Day & Gentner (2007) Nonintentional analogical inference in text comprehension
finding: Known only from the title: analogical inferences can arise during ordinary reading without being asked for.
numbers: Not read. The PDF is a scan with no text layer and no OCR tool was available.
limits: Not verified. Follow up.
agent_relevance: Possible: unrequested conjectures may carry over; the O7 check may need to run even when no analogy was asked for.
